history.value: Chase Coleman founded Tiger Global in New York in 2001 as Tiger Technology, a technology hedge fund backed by his mentor Julian Robertson; it began investing in private companies in 2003. Its private bets on Facebook, LinkedIn, JD.com and Flipkart made its name. Its private funds, the newest targeting $2.2 billion, hold at least $31 billion of the $78 billion the firm manages; the track record on this page covers the private investments only.
history.basis: Founding year, city, founder, the Tiger Technology name, Julian Robertson's backing and the long/short technology start are the firm's own Our Story page (read 2026-09-29: 'In 2001, Tiger Global, originally named Tiger Technology, was founded by Chase Coleman at age 25, with backing from his mentor Julian Robertson'; 'Headquartered in New York, Tiger Global launched with a long/short public equity strategy to invest in leading global technology companies'; 'By 2003 ... the firm expanded into private investing'), corroborated by ADV Schedule A (Coleman, member since 03/2001) and the first private fund's paper Form D (Tiger Technology Private Investment Partners, EDGAR index 2003-08-18). The four bets are the first four of the page's own 'Notable examples'; the Facebook and LinkedIn shares were bought privately in 2009 to 2011, partly through the FB Partners and LinkedIn Holdings vehicles (decisions.md D6, D8), and Forbes reported the Facebook trade made about $1 billion (2013-02-14, cited by Wikipedia). PENDING: confirm the four are member rows once the base lands. The newest fund is Private Investment Partners 17: launch letter 2025-12-08 with a $2.2 billion target (TechCrunch 2025-12-08); its own Form D of 2026-03-20 reported nothing sold yet. The asset figures are the ADV's (annual amendment 2026-03-27): regulatory assets $77,993,959,953 and at least $31,536,376,225 in the private-equity funds (the aum field's floor; PIP XI's value is unknown, see aum). Moved off the page: the public-equity business (long/short, long-only and crossover funds, about $41.6 billion in its master funds) is the other strategy desk and is not part of the portfolio shown (decisions.md D2, D3); the second office in San Francisco and the advisers in Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia and Shanghai; Scott Shleifer ran private investing from 2003 until January 2024 (senior adviser since); PIP XV ($12.7 billion, 2021 to 2022) was the largest fund; the 2022 losses; the site's '30 countries' and '90 portfolio company IPOs'.

investment_concept.value: “Tiger Global is a research-driven investment firm pursuing a long-term approach to partnering with high-quality, innovative companies across different stages of their lifecycle.”
investment_concept.basis: The firm's own statement, verbatim: the first sentence of the homepage H1 (read 2026-09-29, sources/site/home-2026-09-29.html); no edit was needed. The H1's second sentence is in the firm's first person: 'With more than 25 years of experience, we aim to identify and invest in the best companies in the world.' Competing lines on the same site: the Our Story H2, 'We invest in the defining companies of the future.'; the homepage meta description, 'Tiger Global is a research-driven investment firm with 25+ years of experience investing in the defining companies of the future.'

investment_stage.basis: The firm's own words: 'Our private equity business invests in early through late-stage companies', crosswalked to Seed, Series A and Growth; reconciled against the landed entry stages (Growth 354, Series A 120, Seed 16, Pre-Seed 2, undetermined 69 of 561): a growth-weighted book with a real early-stage share.

investment_geo.basis: Derived from hq_country on the landed base of 561 companies (the firm publishes no geography filter): US 267 (47.6%), India 113 (20.1%), China 27, Brazil 24, Israel 14, UK 14, Australia 9, Canada 8, Singapore 8, Germany 8, France 7, Colombia 6; Latin America (Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, Argentina, Chile) and Europe each about 7%.

investment_scope.basis: Derived from the grind's focus column on the landed base (the firm publishes no sector vocabulary; the Thrive precedent), keeping sectors with at least 25 companies (about 4.5% of 561 rows): Consumer & Marketplaces 159, SaaS 103, Fintech & Payments 92, Industrial & Robotics 34, Healthcare & Bio 27, Media, Gaming & Advertising 25, Crypto & Web3 22, AI & Applied AI 22, Data Infrastructure 22, DevTools & APIs 21, Security 20, Climate & Energy 7.

investment_range.basis: MEDIAN: press-based. 471 member rows record the size of the round in which Tiger is first named; their median is $53M (10th percentile $12M, 25th $24M, 75th $116M, 90th $275M; Seed $8M, Series A $20M, Growth $80M). It is a ROUND-SIZE PROXY for check size, not Tiger's cheque, and Tiger rarely took the whole round. LOWER LIMIT: the 10th percentile of those rounds ($12M); the firm runs no seed programme. UPPER LIMIT: $500M, the scale of the largest rounds Tiger led in the record (ShareChat's $502M Series E, April 2021), under 5% of PIP XV's $12.7B; larger rounds it joined ($2.5B) are other investors' leads.

notable_investments.basis: The five best known of the firm's companies, most recognised first (PRO-152). Also considered: Stripe, ByteDance, JD.com, Flipkart, Databricks, Waymo.

aum.basis: The private-equity desk's floor, both ends (COLLECTION.md 1, strategy desks; decisions.md D2): the sum of Section 7.B.(1) gross asset values of 25 private-equity master funds on Tiger Global Management, LLC's Form ADV (CRD 160318, annual amendment of 2026-03-27, https://reports.adviserinfo.sec.gov/reports/ADV/160318/PDF/160318.pdf): Private Investment Partners V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, XII, XIV, XV and XVI ($30,180,985,570) and the 15 PIP 1 co-investment vehicles, PIP 1 LLC to 1-T ($1,355,390,655). Feeders are left out because their assets sit in their masters (PIP XV Feeder $3,181,662,453; PIP XVI Feeder $859,246,231). PIP XI is left out, which makes this a floor: its section repeats PIP XII's block to the dollar ($5,508,057,649 gross assets, 559 owners, 8% related persons, 9% funds of funds, 24% non-US, $1,000,000 minimum). Checked on the rendered pages (203 for XI, 210 for XII, data/filings/adv/160318.pdf, text clipped to the page): the duplicate is in the filing itself, not a parse artifact, while each section's name, fund ID, general partner and Form D file number are its own. The block is XII's: the adviser's 2023-10-11 amendment (the same report as captured at https://web.archive.org/web/20231108100855/https://reports.adviserinfo.sec.gov/reports/ADV/160318/PDF/160318.pdf) shows XII at $4,972,244,226 with 556 owners, 9% funds of funds and 24% non-US, and XI at $5,826,082,773 with 529 owners, 13% and 17%; closed funds keep their investor mix, and every other private-equity fund's owner count moved by 4 or fewer between the two filings (XII +3 on this reading; XI would be +30, with 13% to 9% funds of funds and 17% to 24% non-US). XI's value at the 2026 amendment is therefore unknown and is not counted. The adviser's Item 5.F regulatory assets, $77,993,959,953 (33 accounts; $54,187,952,415 for non-US clients), cover the public-equity funds as well (master funds Tiger Global Investments $30,183,824,407, Crossover $6,195,942,261 and Long Opportunities $5,263,187,210) and never fill this field. Cross-check: all 29 master funds as filed sum to $78,687,387,752, $693,427,799 above the regulatory assets, which the duplicate explains; without XI they sum to $73,179,330,103, leaving $4,814,629,850 of the regulatory assets for XI and all uncalled commitments together, so the desk's true figure is at most about $36.4 billion. Press put the private-equity business at '$30bn-plus' of a '$58bn' firm in November 2023 (Private Equity Wire 2023-11-22). Parse defect, not fixed here (the file is outside this step): sources/registers/adv-160318.json lists 37 funds, the filing has 38; Tiger Global Private Investment Partners XVI Feeder, L.P. (805-1229772137, $859,246,231, 93 owners) is missing because its name starts page 233 apart from its question label. It is a feeder, so the floor is unchanged.

funds.basis: The private-equity desk's Private Investment Partners series, I (2003) to XVII (2026); there is no XIII. Sizes are the amount sold on each master fund's own Form D where the fund raised directly and filed electronically (VI to XVI; each entry's accession is asserted against TOTALAMOUNTSOLD at build). I to V predate electronic Form D (EDGAR carries only REGDEX index entries for their paper filings), so their sizes are the committed capital in the Palico table Wikipedia cites, flagged as aggregator figures in each note, and II has neither a size nor a reliable year. Vintage is the year of the first sale on the fund's own Form D (the paper filing's index date for I, III, IV and V). XVII's filing reports $0 sold, so it carries no accession and no size. Feeders are described, not listed or added: PIP XV Feeder ($3,418,080,500) and PIP XVI Feeder ($622,645,000) invest in their masters, and XVII Feeder filed with XVII. Counted here, not listed: the PIP 1 co-investment series (Tiger Global PIP 1 LLC, $354,998,623 sold to 55 investors in 2021, and PIP 1-A LLC, $223,662,938 to 60; 15 vehicles, 1 to 1-T, on the 2026 ADV holding $1,355,390,655); the partner and holding vehicles of PIP VIII (2014) and PIP X (2017); the single-deal holdcos Tiger Global FB Partners, LLC (2011, $60,392,506 sold to 16 investors) and Tiger Global LinkedIn Holdings, LLC (2011, Form 3 only); the Singapore 'Internet Fund' and 'Tiger Global <n> Holdings' companies that hold the Indian and Asian positions (decisions.md D2, D8); third-party access feeders (decisions.md D5). The public-equity funds are the other strategy desk and are not listed (decisions.md D2): Tiger Global, L.P. (2001), Tiger Global, Ltd. (2002), Tiger Global II, L.P. and the Tiger Global Investments master; Long Opportunities (2013); Long Opportunities II, formerly Internet Opportunities (2015); Crossover (2021).
